connection: Session 18 provides the prerequisite vocabulary. This session develops dependency boundaries through a focused TimeLedger change.
objectives: Explain why constructor injection makes required collaborators explicit and points high-level workflow code toward abstractions.
Trace control and data across the new API boundary.
Implement dependency direction and constructor injection in the canonical application.
Prove the contract with focused and regression tests.

preQuiz.prompt: Which statement accurately frames dependency direction and constructor injection?

Every implementation must expose all internal details

preQuiz.prompt: Where should a required collaborator be supplied?
options: At an explicit construction or method boundary
preQuiz.explanation: Explicit boundaries make dependencies visible and testable.

options: It names the expected cause and effect

concept.title: Name the contract
paragraphs: The governing rule is that constructor injection makes required collaborators explicit and points high-level workflow code toward abstractions.
Start with what callers need to know, then keep incidental implementation details behind the boundary.
concept.code:
TimeLedgerService service = new(repository, policy);
Result<decimal> result = service.Record(entry);

concept.title: Trace dependencies and control
paragraphs: Follow calls from the public operation through each collaborator or transformation.
A clear direction reduces branching, duplication, and accidental coupling.
concept.code:
// Read the pipeline from caller to result.
TimeLedgerService service = new(repository, policy);

concept.title: Make behavior executable
paragraphs: Focused tests demonstrate the new rule with small deterministic values.
The complete suite then confirms the cumulative application still honors earlier contracts.

lab.objective: Add a compact TimeLedger example for dependency direction and constructor injection.
lab.startingCondition: Sessions 01–18 are complete and all existing tests pass.
steps: Predict the successful path and one boundary or failure case.
Add src/TimeLedger.Domain/TimeLedgerService.cs with a narrow public contract.
Add tests/TimeLedger.Domain.Tests/TimeLedgerServiceTests.cs for the prediction and boundary case.
Run the focused tests and inspect the observed values or control flow.
Run the full Release build and test suite.
lab.expectedBehavior: The new tests establish that constructor injection makes required collaborators explicit and points high-level workflow code toward abstractions; prior behavior remains unchanged.
lab.validation: dotnet build TimeLedger.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test TimeLedger.sln --configuration Release

expectedFiles.why: Provide the canonical dependency boundaries example.
Verify the contract and its boundary case.
Publish synchronized lesson, lab, and quiz material.

commit: session-19: teach dependency direction and constructor injection
review: The public API states one coherent responsibility.
Dependencies and state changes are explicit.
The example remains deterministic and compact.
Tests cover success and a meaningful boundary.

postQuiz.prompt: What did the implementation prove about dependency direction and constructor injection?
options: constructor injection makes required collaborators explicit and points high-level workflow code toward abstractions
Every caller needs concrete implementation details
postQuiz.explanation: The passing tests make the stated rule observable.

postQuiz.prompt: Why keep the public contract narrow?
options: To reduce coupling and preserve implementation freedom
postQuiz.explanation: A narrow contract communicates capability without leaking unrelated details.

options: Only the newest file can compile
postQuiz.explanation: Earlier instructional guarantees must remain true after each session.

reflections: Which boundary in this session carries the most design responsibility?
How does the test reveal cause and effect rather than just a final value?
What implementation detail can change without affecting callers?
whatBreaks: Removing TimeLedgerService.cs removes the executable model for dependency boundaries. Removing its tests permits contract regressions. If the boundary leaks its implementation details, callers become harder to change and isolated testing loses value.
summary: This session established that constructor injection makes required collaborators explicit and points high-level workflow code toward abstractions. The application change and tests preserve that model as executable documentation.
